newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew stood down, relief team to repair ship.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew stood down, relief team to repair ship.

text.p: Risky repairs to the crippled Mir space station will be left to a relief crew next month, Russian officials said on Monday after telling the weary and accident-prone cosmonauts now on board to stand down.

Deputy mission director Igor Goncharov said commander Vasily Tsibliyev, who has developed stress-related heart trouble, and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin would keep the stricken craft ticking over in Earth orbit until they hand over to replacements Anatoly Solovyov and Pavel Vinogradov in about two weeks.

"It was decided to hand over the repairs to the next crew. The repairs will be undertaken after the present crew leaves on August 14," Goncharov told a briefing. The two Russians now on board had been due to return to Earth on August 26.
Solovyov and Vinogradov, who will no longer take French scientist Leopold Eyharts along due to the need to repair Mir's power system, blast off on August 5 for the two-day trip to Mir.
That gives them a week to take over the controls.

NASA physicist Michael Foale, who had been preparing to step in and take Tsibliyev's place in the two-man repair team after the commander fell ill, is not due to leave Mir until mid-September, when he will return to Earth aboard a U.S. Shuttle.

The decision was taken during a meeting of top Russian space officials on Monday. It had been widely expected since the latest calamity hit Mir last Thursday when a tired crewman crashed the on-board computer by pulling out a wrong cable.
Eyharts, due to spend only three weeks on Mir, had also been expected to stay behind as the damage would severely limit his work. Goncharov said he would probably now go in January.

Lazutkin, 39, and Tsibliyev, 43, had hoped to carry out repairs to Mir's electric cables last week but Tsibliyev developed an irregular heartbeat as stress began to tell after a series of problems struck Mir. Mission Control first delayed the job to the end of this week and then asked Foale to step in.

The crew have been limping through space since an unmanned cargo craft being manoeuvred by Tsibliyev collided with the station's Spektr scientific module on June 25, punching a small hole in it and smashing one of its four solar power panels.

Only split-second thinking saved the three men aboard as air hissed out of the puncture. Spektr was sealed off. But shutting the hatches meant also disconnected the module's three undamaged solar panels, cutting Mir's electricity supply by up to half.

Solovyov and Vinogradov will have to go into the cramped and airless Spektr wearing bulky spacesuits to reconnect the cabling. They have also been in training at Star City near Moscow to repair the original puncture, probably on a spacewalk.
Goncharov, who is mission doctor, said Foale, 40, and Lazutkin were in good health, while Tsibliyev showed no more signs of the irregular heartbeat that showed up a week ago.

The two Russians, who have been on board since February and have coped with a jinx-like series of problems including a major fire and a breakdown in the oxygen generator, were starting to prepare for a return to Earth's gravity, Goncharov said.

The crew were also preparing to make some repairs to the temperature control system, which was presently allowing for the temperature to vary from 16 to 25 degrees Celsius (61 to 75 Fahrenheit) in different parts of the sprawling space complex.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin had a video link-up with Earth at the weekend. Foale will be able to chat with his family on Monday, officials at Mission Control said on Monday.
"I have to brush my teeth before that," reporters heard Foale, a British-born astrophysicist, telling operators during a radio link-up with Mission Control on Monday morning.
